text:
Introduction

This guidance updates guidance first published in 2013 to:

reflect changes to the professional regulation of public health specialists from backgrounds other than medicine

provide additional information about joint appointments

reflect changes to guidance, policy and organisational responsibilities

Purpose of this guidance

Context

Since 1 April 2013, every upper-tier and unitary local authority has had a legal duty to take steps to improve the public’s health in its area. These authorities have taken on critical public health functions, and provide local leadership for public health underpinned by statutory functions, dedicated resources and an expert public health team. This means that upper-tier and unitary local authorities are responsible for appointing and employing consultants in public health. In the NHS, these consultants are subject to the consultant appointment processes set out in The National Health Service (Appointment of Consultants) Regulations 1996.

What this guidance covers

This guidance sets out a good practice standard. Posts recruited in line with this standard may be endorsed by the Faculty of Public Health. Employers can refer to this endorsement in job adverts and recruitment materials to show that the post meets the expected standard for a consultant in public health appointment. Employers should not advertise or describe a post as a consultant in public health post unless it has been endorsed through the process set out in this guidance. This provides reassurance to applicants and to the public served by these posts that they meet the quality and standards expected of consultants in public health.

There is separate good practice guidance for appointing consultants in the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) and the Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC). These organisations have their own internal arrangements, led by their relevant public health workforce or professional standards teams.

The recruitment process described in this guidance has been developed to maintain a national standard for the appointment of consultants in public health and consultants in academic public health. It does this by reflecting the process in The National Health Service (Appointment of Consultants) Regulations 1996 that is used in medical and dental consultant posts in the NHS. The regulations do not apply to appointments for:

local authorities

strategic authorities (for example, a mayoral combined authority or a county combined authority)

higher education institutions

However, it is a well-established convention that posts that are open both to medically qualified people and to people from backgrounds other than medicine (for example, the majority of appointments in public health) should follow similar processes, even though they fall outside the regulatory framework.

Each organisation is responsible for complying with any legal requirements relating to recruitment and employment. This guidance should be interpreted alongside existing local authority recruitment arrangements for posts of this seniority. Higher education institutions should interpret it alongside any guidance on the recruitment of clinical academics.

This guidance is not legally binding and is not designed to explain the law. Employers should also refer to:

The National Health Service (Appointment of Consultants) Regulations 1996 to understand how these regulations work as an equivalent process in the NHS

any other relevant guidance on the employment of senior post holders in local authorities or clinical academic positions

This guidance also:

promotes public health as a specialism of choice for registered medical practitioners and people from a background other than medicine

supports employers to encourage consultant and academic workforce flexibility to ensure specialists have opportunities to develop knowledge, skills and experience across the different areas of public health practice

ensures that the recruitment and selection procedure demonstrates a positive image of the recruiting organisation

supports the recruitment of appropriately skilled people to enable the organisation to achieve its aims and objectives

sets out objective, fair and transparent recruitment practices throughout public health

ensures that selection decisions are based on objective and justifiable criteria

supports the maintenance of recruitment methods that are cost effective and efficient

supports the principles of joint working between higher education institutions and the health service as set out in the Follett Report (Review of Appraisal, Disciplinary and Reporting Arrangements for Senior NHS and University Staff with Academic and Clinical Duties), which is equally applicable to local authorities

Directors of public health in local authorities are joint appointments between the Secretary of State and the local authority. There is separate guidance on the role of the director of public health, their accountability and their appointment.

Requirements for consultant in public health appointments

Appointees to consultant in public health posts in local authorities should be able to demonstrate competence across all areas of specialist public health practice. The Faculty of Public Health requires appointees to be qualified as public health specialists and to be on the General Medical Council (GMC), General Dental Council (GDC) or UK Public Health Register (UKPHR) specialist register. Appointees must also undertake the required continuing professional development (CPD) and revalidation. GMC registrants must also hold a licence to practise.

The Faculty of Public Health expects those invited to interview to meet its standards, including being up to date with their CPD. The Faculty of Public Health also expects applicants to be members of the Faculty of Public Health, either as a fellow of the Faculty of Public Health (FFPH) or as a member of the Faculty of Public Health (MFPH). However, this is not a requirement for appointment, unlike the requirements to hold GMC, GDC or UKPHR specialist registration.

Public health specialists can be medically qualified or from backgrounds other than medicine and may work across the breadth of public health practice in different employers. It is therefore recommended that employers seek parity, using established or equivalent terms and conditions for consultants in public health across public health employers. Mobility across sectors and employers within the public health workforce is critical to:

develop the pipeline of future senior public health leadership

support workforce flexibility

retain a broad base of experience and improve system resilience

Most public health consultant posts are open to all specialist registrants in public health. In the extremely rare circumstances where the employer believes that a post might be restricted to only some registered persons, this should be discussed with the Faculty of Public Health registrar, as the person responsible for professional standards and good public health practice in the workforce. See appendix A for information on the professional requirements relating to the appointment of a consultant in public health.

Designing the consultant role

The Faculty of Public Health provides a template job description and person specification for use in consultant in public health appointments in local authorities and consultant in academic public health positions. Some local authorities may use alternative titles for these positions in line with other job titles in the authority, such as assistant director of public health or head of service. However, a Faculty of Public Health-approved job description and person specification should be used if the post is to have the title ‘consultant in public health’. See the faculty website for job descriptions.

To support national consistency for roles at this level, employers should incorporate the full contents of the Faculty of Public Health’s template into their local job description format. For higher education institutions, this should also reflect the Follett principles. The principles are a set of management guidelines governing the employment of clinical academics who work jointly for the NHS and higher education institutions which can be adapted for other employers. These should be adapted with reference to the appropriate honorary contract and joint working arrangements made with both the employer and the institution holding the honorary contract. NHS Employers and the Universities and Colleges Employers Association have produced guidance on the Follett principles for higher education institutions and NHS provider organisations. This also provides a useful framework for other organisations entering into joint working or honorary contract arrangements.

Employers should include the qualification and registration requirements in the job description and on the application form, and candidates, if shortlisted, should be asked to bring the relevant proof to the interview.

Joint appointments

Some local authorities use joint appointments or secondment arrangements for consultants in public health with integrated care boards (ICBs), NHS trusts, NHS foundation trusts or other local authorities as part of joint or integrated working arrangements (for examples, see appendix B). These arrangements may have specific statutory requirements for appointment and employment processes, which should be considered when designing such roles.

When designing a joint role, employers should give practical arrangements the same attention as the job design. These arrangements support effective recruitment and induction and should be agreed between employing organisations through a memorandum of understanding or service level agreement. Considerations should include:

office working locations

allowance for travel time and mileage between workplaces

meeting attendance requirements

time management

IT access

line management and professional lines of accountability

interactions with wider system partners

deputising arrangements and team support across employing organisations

Using interim or locum consultant appointments

Where it is not possible to make a permanent appointment (for example, the appointment is to cover a period of parental leave or long-term illness), employers may choose to use an interim, fixed-term appointment, or use a locum through an agency for up to 6 months. However, this is not recommended as a long-term solution to a vacancy.

When making temporary appointments, employers should ensure that the interim or locum consultant meets the required standard for the role and is assessed by an appointments committee that includes at least 2 public health professionals. This is to prevent issues such as ‘fitness to practise’ concerns or failure to maintain good public health practice. These issues disproportionately occur when locum and interim arrangements are used without applying the same process as substantive posts. The recruiting manager (usually the director of public health) and the HR department should work together to ensure:

the person holds the required specialist registration (set out in the standard Faculty of Public Health person specification)

the person is in current good professional standing with the Faculty of Public Health (if a member)

references have been checked prior to the consultant starting in post

if the person is working for an NHS body or providing services to NHS bodies, the registered health professional is not the subject of a Health Professional Alert Notice (HPAN)

Although not mandatory, it is good practice to hold an advisory appointments committee (AAC) and involve a faculty assessor in the selection process for an interim or locum post (see AAC section below).

If an interim or locum appointment is extended for up to a further 6 months, the Faculty of Public Health sets out that this should only follow a satisfactory review by the employing organisations and consultation with the Faculty of Public Health adviser. Employers are advised to notify the Faculty of Public Health of their intention to extend the appointment at an early stage, to ensure that:

a plan can be made to support a permanent appointment

a job description can be re-approved by the faculty adviser in good time

The role of the faculty adviser

On behalf of the Faculty of Public Health, the regional faculty adviser approves:

the job description

the essential and desirable criteria in the person specification

the recruitment material for new and replacement consultant posts

This helps ensure that job descriptions, person specifications and supporting documentation are appropriate and meet agreed standards for good public health practice, statutory requirements and other good practice. Once approved by the faculty adviser, the Faculty of Public Health requires that the job description is not changed. See the faculty website for a list of the regional faculty advisers.

The faculty adviser will provide feedback to the local authority or university. This may cover:

areas of responsibility

staff management

budget responsibilities

local working arrangements

possible future developments for the post

Once the job description and person specification are approved, the regional faculty adviser will send an approval letter to the Faculty of Public Health office. The letter will confirm to the faculty assessor that the post has been approved. The AAC reference number will be provided to the employer by the Faculty of Public Health’s national office. The employer can then convene its AAC.

If a local authority or university does not already have a working relationship with a faculty adviser, it should establish one at the start of the recruitment and selection process. Contact details for all the Faculty of Public Health advisers are available on the Faculty of Public Health’s website.

Employers can also seek advice from DHSC regional public health teams. Where needed, Faculty of Public Health and DHSC regional teams will support the employer to develop a job description and person specification that both organisations can endorse as consultant-level.

Advisory appointments committee

An advisory appointments committee (AAC) provides a rigorous and well-established method for assuring the technical and professional skills required for senior medical appointments. The AAC can reduce the risk to both the public and the employer of making an inappropriate appointment. These committees can take place in person or online. Where they take place in person, employers are expected to meet the reasonable travel and subsistence expenses of the external assessor.

The AAC assesses the qualifications, experience, capability and competence of prospective consultants through a variety of methods, including stakeholder panels, technical interviews and psychometric testing. These methods are likely to be familiar to local authorities and higher education institutions and are a normal part of recruitment and selection at this senior level.

The employer should convene an AAC in accordance with the recruitment policies and procedures of the employer. An AAC can vary from the recommended constitution in the National Health Service (Appointment of Consultants) Regulations 1996, as these do not apply to local authorities or higher education institutions. Any variations should ensure that a panel has the right knowledge and experience to assess consultants from a range of backgrounds, or to reflect local circumstances. For instance, where the Public Health team reports into another executive director or where they will be working closely with the NHS or the voluntary sector, they could also form part of the AAC.

For an appointment to be approved by the Faculty of Public Health, the committee must include at least one external professional assessor appointed after consultation with the Faculty of Public Health, often known as the faculty assessor. Otherwise, the post cannot use the consultant in public health title or rely on the status associated with consultant-level public health appointments.

More faculty assessors can be added if the recruiting employer agrees. Where a clinical academic appointment includes a Follett-style honorary contract, the body holding the honorary contract should also be engaged in the process.

In addition to the external assessor, an AAC would normally include:

either the chief executive of the local authority or the vice-chancellor of the university (or a nominated representative)

either a consultant in public health from the employing organisation or, if none is available, a consultant from another specialty or neighbouring organisation

either the director of public health of the employing authority or for a university a person at an equivalent functional and managerial level. Alternatively, the DHSC regional director of public health or their nominated representative

an external professional assessor, appointed after consultation with the Faculty of Public Health. The faculty will provide names of assessors who are geographically separate from the recruiting organisation

a lay member with an interest in public health who is neither a public health specialist nor an employee of the organisation. In a local authority, this can be an elected councillor responsible for public health

Local authorities and higher education institutions should have regard to this list when deciding the 5 core members of the appointment committee. The employing organisation may appoint additional members as it considers appropriate.

The Academy of Medical Royal Colleges has agreed that faculty assessors may double as the university representative on an AAC for university and consultant appointments where all parties agree. However, the academy has also ruled that the reverse would not be acceptable; that is, university representatives may not double as faculty assessors. If such an arrangement is necessary, it should be agreed in advance with the Faculty of Public Health and with an appropriate assessor nominated by the faculty.

Where a joint appointment is made between 2 employers, careful consideration should be given to the membership of the AAC, as the employers should act as a single authority for this purpose. The employers should jointly appoint one lay member and one external professional assessor. Each employer should also appoint at least one member who meets the requirements for the chief executive or nominated representative, the director of public health, and a public health consultant, as set out above. One authority should appoint 2 of these members, with the other appointing the third. If there are more than 2 employers, the appointments should be allocated across each employer.

Each member should be clear about their role on the committee and how to participate professionally and in compliance with the employer’s recruitment, selection and equality policies and procedures.

When considering which candidate or candidates to recommend for appointment, the committee’s overriding consideration should be to recommend the best candidate for the post. Selection should be based solely on the candidate’s suitability for the post when compared with the person specification.

Committees should always make a clear recommendation on the most suitable candidate, if any, for appointment by the employer. This recommendation or decision will be made in accordance with local procedures. As the AAC should be the final stage of the recruitment process, the Faculty of Public Health expects the employer to appoint the candidate recommended by the AAC. However, it remains advisory. Where exceptional circumstances mean this is not possible, this should be discussed with the AAC.

The employer should agree the approach to expenses relating to the AAC before the committee meets.

Internal processes

There can be circumstances where an internal process may be acceptable to the Faculty of Public Health. The employer should always contact the registrar of the Faculty of Public Health to seek their agreement to a post not being advertised externally. To contact the registrar, email registrar@fph.org.uk.

What employers need to do before recruitment

Planning for the appointment should begin as early as possible to ensure the full engagement of all parties who will add value to the outcome. It is important to plan the timetable for the whole process at the outset, so that everyone involved - management, HR, specialist advisers and potential applicants - understands the timetable.

Given the range of members on the appointment committee, the timetable for appointment should not be confirmed until after prospective members have been contacted and availability ascertained.

Timeline of standard recruitment process

9 weeks before the AAC meets:

the employer sends the job description, person specification and advert to the faculty adviser. See the faculty website for a list of faculty advisers

the faculty adviser advises on any changes needed and sends the employer an approval letter by email within 3 weeks. The approved documents are then valid for 6 months. If the documents need updating, the employer should contact the regional adviser and AAC team

6 weeks before the AAC meets:

the employer contacts the Faculty of Public Health with:

approval letter from the Faculty of Public Health regional adviser

job description

AAC details, for example, the date of the panel

the Faculty of Public Health provides the employer with a list of suitable faculty assessors to contact and the reference number for the AAC

the employer advertises the post in at least 2 professional and nationally distributed journals (for example, the British Medical Journal or the Health Service Journal (HSJ))

the employer should also advertise the job online on pages such as NHS jobs or the Faculty of Public Health jobs board

the employer finalises the AAC panel composition and informs the faculty assessor of attendance arrangements for the AAC

3 weeks before the AAC meets:

the employer sends all applications to AAC members, including the faculty assessor for shortlisting, together with:

documentary evidence of applicants’ eligibility and a list of AAC panel members and their roles

the agreed job description and/or person specification and instructions for the shortlisting process

the employer invites shortlisted candidates and finalises arrangements for the AAC panel

the Faculty of Public Health checks candidates’ good professional standing

the employer checks whether any reasonable adjustments are needed for the AAC and interview

Day of the AAC:

the AAC panel meets, with the faculty assessor attending, and makes a recommendation to the employer

the panel gives feedback to candidates

the employer provides an expenses form for faculty assessors on the day

1 week after the AAC meets:

the faculty assessor returns the report form and notifies the Faculty of Public Health of the outcome of the panel

if the post needs to be re-advertised, the employer should contact their regional adviser and AAC team

Advertising the post

Employers should choose advertising methods and media that attract the widest possible field of suitably qualified candidates. Subject to local authority and university policies on advertising posts, employers should advertise posts in at least 2 places, reflecting the requirement in The National Health Service (Appointment of Consultants) Regulations 1996 for medical and dental consultant appointments in the NHS.

Typically, advertisements are placed in nationally distributed journals normally associated with such posts - for example, the British Medical Journal or HSJ - and relevant sector jobs boards (see below). This will increase the chances of attracting suitably qualified applicants from established professional networks.

Jobs boards

The following are widely used for advertising posts:

Faculty of Public Health jobs board - most relevant for specialist public health roles across local government, the NHS, academia and national public health bodies. Useful for consultant in public health posts and roles requiring specialist registration

NHS Jobs - most relevant for NHS organisations, ICBs, NHS provider collaboratives and roles hosted by NHS employers. However, it is widely used by local authorities and other public health employers. Useful where the post is NHS-employed or closely linked to NHS services

BMJ Careers - most relevant for medically qualified applicants and consultant-level medical roles. Useful for posts open to public health doctors or where employers want to reach a medical consultant audience

HSJ Jobs - most relevant for senior health management, NHS leadership, commissioning, provider and system roles. Useful for public health posts with a strong health service, partnership or system leadership focus

Jobs.ac.uk - most relevant for higher education institutions, research organisations and clinical academic roles. Useful for consultant in academic public health posts and public health academic appointments

LG Jobs - most relevant for local authority roles. Useful for consultant, assistant director, public health specialist and senior public health posts employed by councils

Public Health Jobs - most relevant for dedicated public health roles across local government, the NHS, charities, academia and consultancy. Useful for reaching candidates already searching for public health specialist roles

In the interests of equity, all posts should be open to application by all suitably registered candidates. In the extremely rare circumstances where the employer believes that a post might be restricted to only some registered persons, this should be discussed with the faculty registrar.

Roles in the appointment of consultants in public health

DHSC’s role in appointing a consultant in public health

DHSC, through its regional public health teams, can support the employer in ensuring a robust and appropriate recruitment and selection process that supports them in recruiting the best candidate for the role. Regional directors of public health or their nominated representative can work with local government and academia in any area where there is a consultant vacancy to ensure a robust and transparent appointment process is established and a timescale for recruitment and appointment agreed.

DHSC can:

work with the employer to confirm that the local job description has the necessary technical and professional skills required and has appropriate public health responsibility and accountability for a consultant role, before it is agreed by the faculty adviser

offer advice in relation to the recruitment and selection process, including the appointment of Faculty of Public Health assessors

if required, provide a senior professionally qualified member of DHSC to participate in the local AAC

where participating in the committee, support the local authority to verify that their preferred candidate has the necessary specialist public health qualifications, skills and experience and appropriate registration to undertake the role

The role of the faculty in appointing a consultant in public health

The Faculty of Public Health oversees the quality of training and professional development of consultants in public health in the UK and sets the professional standards in the discipline. The Faculty of Public Health embraces the wider multidisciplinary public health workforce. It also provides advice on CPD, appraisals, revalidation, good practice and practitioner development.

External professional assessment and advice provided by the Faculty of Public Health checks that consultants in public health have the necessary technical and professional skills to promote, improve and protect health and provide credible advice to the NHS about public health in relation to health services.

This is based on the Faculty of Public Health’s role in setting training, professional development and standards and its ability to provide independent assessment and advice to local authorities on these issues.

The role of the Faculty of Public Health and faculty adviser in the appointment process is to:

provide advice to the employer on the consultant job description, advert and person specification and to give a definitive opinion as to whether they fulfil the technical and professional elements required to protect and improve health and provide advice on health services

provide a list of representatives of the Faculty of Public Health for the employer to approach to act as an assessor to sit on the AAC for every consultant appointment to assess and advise on the necessary technical and professional skills, qualifications and professional registration issues

As part of its appointment procedures, the Faculty of Public Health requires that the faculty assessor is involved in the shortlisting of candidates to ensure that they meet the professional qualifications and requirements for a consultant in public health ahead of interview. The faculty assessors will act as the link with the Faculty of Public Health who will carry out validation checks on whether the applicants meet the professional qualifications and requirements to fulfil the role. This usually takes less than one working day to carry out.

Regional faculty advisers can assist by:

identifying the appropriate type of assessor for the role being appointed, for example, where their background or experience aligns with the role being recruited to

confirming to the local authority or higher education institution through validation checks whether their preferred candidate has the necessary specialist public health skills to undertake the role

confirming whether specialist registrars are within 6 months of completing their training and due to receive their certificate of completion of training, and are therefore eligible to be shortlisted

providing evidence to the employer before interviews take place if, following validation checks, a candidate does not have the specialist public health qualifications, skills and registration needed to undertake the role

The role of the employer associations in appointing a consultant in public health

The Local Government Association (LGA) and the Universities and Colleges Employers Association provide sector-specific advice on issues relating to recruitment processes and pay, terms and conditions of employment.

Appendix A: essential professional requirements for consultants in public health

Professional regulation

Consultants in public health from backgrounds other than medicine are registered with the UKPHR.

Medical and dental public health consultants are regulated by GMC and GDC.

The following routes of specialist training and assessment provide assurance of competence:

undertaking Faculty of Public Health specialty training and obtaining a certificate of completion of training for registrants from backgrounds other than medicine, and medical and dental backgrounds

demonstrating competence by submitting a retrospective portfolio that is assessed and approved by the Faculty of Public Health (for admission to the GMC specialist register) or the UKPHR (for admission to the UKPHR register)

Any appointment to a consultant in public health or consultant in academic public health post in line with Faculty of Public Health appointment procedures must be of an individual who is either:

on the GMC full and specialist register with a licence to practise in:

public health medicine

a specialty other than public health and able to demonstrate equivalent training or appropriate experience of public health practice, for example, through the GMC portfolio route

on the GDC specialist list in:

dental public health

a specialty other than dental public health and able to demonstrate equivalent training or appropriate experience of public health practice, for example, through the GMC portfolio route

on the UKPHR for public health specialists

a public health specialty registrar who is currently on the UK public health training programme and not yet on the GMC, GDC or UKPHR specialist register, and who can provide verifiable signed documentary evidence that they are within 6 months of gaining entry to a register at the date of interview

Note that applicants going through the portfolio registration routes (GMC or UKPHR) are not eligible to be shortlisted for interview until they are included on the register. The 6-month rule does not apply to these portfolio route applicants.

Revalidation

Revalidation is the process by which UKPHR and GMC public health registrants demonstrate that they have met their required professional standards, including:

CPD

quality improvement activity

annual professional appraisal

reflective practice

Employers should note that, for GMC registrants, revalidation is a requirement to maintain their licence to practise. Registrants are required to maintain a link to:

a designated body (a UK healthcare organisation approved by the GMC to oversee the revalidation and clinical governance of licensed doctors)

a responsible officer (a senior doctor appointed by a designated body to oversee the professional conduct, annual appraisal and revalidation of its medical staff)

Licensed doctors should use the GMC connection tool to find out their revalidation connection type.

Responsible officers in Great Britain are responsible for revalidation recommendations to GMC in respect of individual doctors.

Both UKPHR and GMC publish guidance and resources on the revalidation process. While the requirements are broadly similar, the approaches to revalidation vary slightly between UKPHR and GMC, and employers should consult the relevant regulator’s guidance on revalidation.

DHSC acts as the designated body for revalidation for:

GMC registrants, where appropriate, for all doctors for whom it is the employing organisation

doctors employed by local government

Employers should note that there is an ongoing time commitment required of consultants in public health to revalidate and maintain their fitness to practise. This time commitment should be reflected in the consultant’s job plan (or similar document) and guidance is available in the following section.

Professional appraisal and continuing professional development

CPD plays an important role in maintaining professional standards and quality for all professional groups in local government and in academia. It is an essential feature of the revalidation and re-registration processes for consultants in public health and specialists. In public health, the overall aim of CPD is to ensure that those who work in the field develop and maintain the necessary knowledge, skills and attributes to practise effectively and work towards improving the health of the population.

CPD is a professional obligation for all public health professionals, including consultants, and protected time to undertake CPD activities is a contractual entitlement for those consultants who transferred into local government employment on medical and dental contracts on 1 April 2013.

Employers will wish to consider these issues in relation to the appointment of consultants. To comply with the Faculty of Public Health’s minimum standards for CPD and to remain in good professional standing, consultants must either:

submit a satisfactory CPD return to the Faculty of Public Health for the previous CPD year, 1 April to 31 March, unless they have been formally exempted by the faculty from this requirement

take part in another CPD scheme which is recognised by the Faculty of Public Health as equivalent

Employers should ensure that all consultants have protected time within their job plan to engage in

CPD

professional appraisal

revalidation

other supporting professional activities, such as being an educational supervisor or professional appraiser

For a full-time consultant there will typically be 7.5 sessions for public health duties and 2.5 sessions for supporting professional activities. This can be averaged, for example, as a full day every other week. Consultants in public health should also have access to a local study budget to support CPD activities, for example, attendance at professional conferences and specialist training or skills refresher events.

The annual process of checking and refreshing professional competence should run alongside the local authority’s mechanisms for:

target setting

performance appraisal

management and leadership development

in many authorities, progression within the relevant salary scheme

For consultants employed by higher education institutions, this is part of the joint appraisal and job planning process (the Follett principles) and professional appraisal prescribed within the honorary contracts.

As part of their revalidation requirements, GMC and UKPHR specialist registrants are required to have an annual professional appraisal, which considers information from across their whole scope of practice and is an integral part of their ongoing professional registration. Local authorities should reassure themselves that they are in a position to support this requirement. This will include any work a specialist does for a local authority and for the higher education institution but is separate to the work-based appraisal between the employer and the post holder.

For joint appointments, it is good practice, in line with the Follett principles, to have a joint work-based appraisal with both employers, factoring in the post holder’s whole scope of work carried out for both employing organisations.

The role of the responsible officer in relation to a consultant in public health

Employers must be aware of The Medical Profession (Responsible Officers) Regulations 2010, which came into force on 1 January 2011. These have implications for employers that employ or contract with licensed doctors. These regulations designate bodies that are required to nominate or appoint a responsible officer for the purposes of medical revalidation. They connect doctors to designated bodies in a strict hierarchy to make a link between an individual doctor and a responsible officer.

The connection for doctors employed by local authorities and higher education institutions is not to the local authority or higher education employer, as these are not designated bodies as defined in The Medical Profession (Responsible Officers) Regulations 2010. DHSC is the statutorily defined designated body for all medical practitioners employed by local authorities. For higher education institutions, this is included in the substantive employment contract arrangements between the employee and the higher education institution and, in the honorary contract with DHSC, UKHSA or NHS England for public health clinical academics.

Where a consultant holds a joint appointment across 2 employers or an honorary contract, GMC provides an online tool that helps doctors determine their connection to a designated body (see the section ‘Revalidation’).

When employing or contracting with licensed doctors, employers should ask them for the name of their designated body and responsible officer in addition to other information.

For advice on the connections for doctors working with local authorities and higher education institutions, email the appraisal and revalidation shared service at revalidation@ukhsa.gov.uk.

Employers need to confirm that the doctor or specialist is registered with the correct body (GMC, GDC or UKPHR) and has no restrictions to practise or ongoing investigations.

Job planning

All consultants in public health should have an annual job plan agreed between the consultant and the employer. The job plan sets out the agreed duties, responsibilities and objectives for the coming year and should include a breakdown of how the consultant’s working time is allocated across their duties and responsibilities. The annual job plan also forms an important part of the submission for the national clinical impact awards, and if employers do not adequately support consultants in job planning, it can prevent medical and dental consultants from applying for the national clinical impact award scheme.

Typically, the working week of a full-time consultant will comprise 10 programmed activities or sessions. The Faculty of Public Health recommends that consultants should be allocated 7.5 sessions per week for public health duties and 2.5 sessions per week for supporting professional activities, with a higher proportion of supporting professional activities for those working part-time. Supporting professional activities include CPD, appraisal and revalidation, teaching and training, research, and other work such as Faculty of Public Health examining or committee work.

See the faculty website for further guidance on job planning.

Pay

Pay scales across the public health system vary between the NHS, civil service, local authorities and higher education institutions. Consultant posts are mobile across the system, therefore, an important consideration for employers will be the ability to recruit and retain this specialist group. Higher education institutions have nationally negotiated higher education pay scales for consultant clinical academic doctors and dentists which take into account market comparability with doctors and dentists working in the NHS. Further information can be obtained from the employing higher education institution or from the Universities and Colleges Employers Association, which represents higher education employers in the relevant annual pay negotiations.

Local authorities should consider the relevant market when deciding the pay, terms and conditions for a role. If market supplements are considered, employers should reference any guidance provided through national negotiating bodies to ensure that equal pay considerations are satisfied. Employers should consider that, where consultants in public health are employed in the NHS, UKHSA or DHSC, they are appointed on either medical and dental terms and conditions for medically qualified consultants or Agenda for Change bands 8d or 9 for consultants from backgrounds other than medicine. Employers will want to consider this when setting pay, terms and conditions to remain competitive in the employment market.

The Public Health Medicine Consultative Committee, a joint committee of the British Medical Association and the Faculty of Public Health, published further advice on employing consultants in public health (PDF, 170KB), including on job evaluation for public health consultant roles that local authorities can consider alongside other technical advice.

Continuity of service

Within local government and the health service, some contractual benefits are normally based on the employee’s length of continuous service, for example, annual leave and enhanced maternity rights. Statutory redundancy entitlements are also based on continuous service, and enhancements above the statutory entitlement are often based on a measure of continuous service. However, although the terms and conditions and ways of measuring continuous service in the health service and local government share some similarities, they are separate and distinct.

Where employees move voluntarily from a health service body to a local authority or the Civil Service and vice versa, there is no obligation on the new employer to recognise service with the previous employer for the purposes of contractual benefits, such as annual leave and for redundancy purposes. Therefore, employees who have built up service and, therefore, associated contractual and redundancy entitlements may be reluctant to move from a health service body to a local authority, and vice versa. This can create a barrier to recruitment and make it difficult for public health specialists to move between public health employers, preventing them from developing experience across the breadth of public health practice.

It is recommended that employers make every effort to recognise past service. In 2015, LGA set out how local authorities can use their current discretionary powers to best effect to recognise past service with NHS or Civil Service bodies where an individual voluntarily takes up a local authority post. This includes supporting continued access to the NHS Pension Scheme with an NHS Pension Direction Order. For guidance on how to make a public health open direction and determination, see the NHS Business Services Authority website, under the section application guidance for a pension direction and/or determination.

Standards for employers of public health teams in England

LGA published the standards for employers of public health teams, which contains further guidance on enabling:

employers to provide a well-led and supportive professional environment

public health professionals to maintain their professionalism

Appendix B: examples of joint appointments

Case study: a joint consultant post between Ealing Community Partners and the London Borough of Ealing council

Background and rationale

Ealing Community Partners identified the need to establish a consultant in public health post to enhance its public health functions. The initiative was strongly supported by the local director of public health, who was actively involved in developing and planning the post at the London Borough of Ealing council. The director of public health funded 25% of the role, with the remainder coming from the trust and the ICB. The primary intention was to strengthen public health activities within the trust, including setting the trust strategy and delivering specific projects focused on the local authority area. The post therefore assists the director of public health in fulfilling the duty to provide public health advice to the NHS. This collaborative approach aims to improve the health of local residents and address health inequalities.

Job design and joint responsibilities

When developing the job description, the trust adopted the standard Faculty of Public Health consultant job template and adapted it to emphasise the joint nature of the appointment. This was then approved by the faculty adviser. The adaptation included explicit duties such as:

participating in local authority and NHS partnership groups, for example, the Joint Strategic Needs Assessment steering group

contributing to local authority workforce development

involvement in the local authority’s major health protection incident response team

providing specialist public health advice on healthcare

These requirements ensured the post holder would operate across both organisational boundaries.

Recruitment and appointment process

The post was advertised on NHS Jobs on NHS terms and conditions by the trust. It attracted a good range of applicants from both medicine and backgrounds other than medicine.

The NHS trust and the local authority ran a joint interview process. A Faculty of Public Health adviser was also included as part of the AAC. This approach was novel for the trust, as it marked the first occasion on which it had appointed a consultant in public health.

Governance, management and professional support

The successful candidate is professionally accountable to the local authority director of public health, while being employed and line-managed by the NHS trust. The director of public health plays an important role in setting the consultant’s objectives and provides ongoing professional support, including agreeing CPD arrangements, supporting preparation for professional appraisal and promoting high standards of public health practice.

To ensure integration with both organisations, the consultant participates in the local authority public health team’s activities, including attendance at senior leadership team meetings and away days, embedding them within the team’s culture and operations. The director of public health has also helped the consultant to connect with wider networks, further supporting their development and effectiveness in the role.

Outcomes and successes

The consultant has effectively worked across both the NHS trust and local authority teams, maintaining integrated responsibilities. The clarity provided in line management, professional accountabilities and the definition of role, purpose, function and funding arrangements has ensured the success of this joint post.

Case study: joint appointment between Wigan council and NHS Wrightington, Wigan and Leigh Hospitals Foundation Trust

Background and rationale

When they took up their roles, the director of public health and deputy director of public health reviewed the public health function within the local authority. At the time, there was limited consultant capacity, and the authority faced challenges in recruiting to these positions because of strong competition for public health roles. Recognising increased interest in integrated roles and the opportunities these bring for strengthening place-based approaches, the leaders used their positive relationship with the local acute trust, which shared similar geographical boundaries with the local authority.

Job design and joint responsibilities

A consultant post was established, fully funded by the local authority but employed by the trust. The job description was developed collaboratively by the director of public health and the trust’s deputy chief executive and approved by the faculty adviser. The appointed consultant leads on health protection and healthcare public health.

The consultant will shortly assume the role of educational supervisor and has helped to establish and shape further joint roles and activity. The position demands significant autonomy, as the consultant works independently within the trust and must manage responsibilities across both organisations.

Professional accountability for the consultant lies with the director of public health, and the consultant is line managed by the deputy chief executive and director of strategy in the trust. Appraisal and revalidation are managed through the trust, with input from the director of public health.

Recruitment and appointment process

The recruitment process was conducted jointly, with two panels comprising the local authority director and deputy director of public health, the director of adult social services, the trust’s deputy chief executive and director of strategy, medical director and nursing director, alongside representatives from the voluntary, community and social enterprise (VCSE) sector and the faculty assessor.

Governance, management and professional support

The post is governed by a memorandum of understanding, which outlines the expectations for the role and each employer. This document details financial flows, procedures for managing departures and dismissals, and practical arrangements such as IT access and physical locations. The memorandum is intended to anticipate and resolve potential challenges or disagreements, ensuring smooth governance. Its development required extensive collaboration between the legal and HR teams of both organisations.

Outcomes and successes

The joint consultant post has now been operational for over a year. It has helped local authority, trust and ICB teams work together. Important outcomes include substantial board-level work addressing health inequalities and supporting public health functions across both organisations, alongside more effective and collaborative system-wide working. The joint consultant post has also provided a practical and sustainable solution to longstanding capacity challenges, enabling the system to share specialist skills more effectively and align efforts around common priorities.
